title: What One Score Hides
scopeNote: This keeps the live model, because impurity has to be manipulated to be understood: move a capacity and watch which tasks notice. Two further capacities, a fourth task, and the prediction stage on which processes each task requires stay in the longer version.
summary: Four capacities feed three executive tasks with different weights, and the three task scores are averaged into one composite. A search finds a different capacity profile with the identical composite, which is the whole argument.
learningObjectives: Explain why no executive task measures a single process.
Explain why averaging impure tasks removes the information that identifies the problem.
Read a pattern across tasks that load differently as evidence about a capacity.
Recognise that two people with the same composite can need different things.
State what a four-capacity model does and does not represent.
interactionTypes: three task scores computed as weighted mixtures, updating live
a composite drawn across the task bars as the average it is
a search that finds a different profile with the identical composite
a spread figure saying whether the composite is hiding anything
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, with each capacity a native range input reporting its value in text. The chart carries a description giving all three task scores, the composite and all four capacity settings, so nothing depends on comparing bar lengths. Task bars and capacity bars are separated by a gap and given their own headings rather than distinguished only by colour, and the composite is drawn as a dashed line across the task bars with its value labelled. The twin search reports both profiles in full text. Where no different profile exists it says so and says what to do instead. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
dataStatus: An invented model with invented weights. Nothing here is a test, a norm, or a description of any person.
simulationNotes: A task score is the weighted mean of the four capacities using that task's weights, and the composite is the unweighted mean of the three task scores. The weights are deliberately different across tasks, because a task loading equally on everything could distinguish nothing. The twin search walks the grid of settings in steps of ten and returns the profile furthest from the current one whose composite ROUNDS to the same number: matching the computed value within a tolerance would let the reported figure move by a point while the note claimed it was identical, which is the kind of small dishonesty the activity is arguing against. The caution states that real tasks do not decompose into four capacities with fixed weights, that the capacities are inferred from performance rather than observed, and that how separable they are is an active argument.
readmeTopic: why a single executive score cannot say what is wrong, and what the pattern across tasks adds
